passage:
Maa,
I'm leaving this on your pillow because I can't say it to your face yet.
On Saturday I told you I was at Sabina's house working on the chemistry model. That's true. We did work on it, from four till six. What I didn't say is that after six we all went up to a birthday party on her building's terrace, and I came home at ten, not eight-thirty like you thought.
When you asked, "How was the studying?" I said, "Good, we finished." Every word was true. I kept telling myself that. But I knew you were picturing me at a desk, and I let you.
I don't want "technically true" to be how we talk. Can we talk tonight?
Pradeep

qa.q: What time did Pradeep come home on Saturday?
qa.a: Pradeep came home at ten, not eight-thirty.

qa.q: Why does Pradeep feel uneasy even though every word was true?
qa.a: Pradeep knew Maa was picturing a desk, not a party, and let her believe it, so the true words still feel like deception.

qa.q: Which step in the letter is a wise one, and why?
qa.a: Pradeep names exactly what was left out and asks to talk tonight, which gives Maa the full picture and starts rebuilding trust.

qa.q: How might Maa feel reading the letter on her pillow?
qa.a: She might feel hurt at being misled about the party, but also relieved that Pradeep chose to tell her.

grounding: A teenager writes to Maa about skipping the party from an account of studying at Sabina's house, seeing that true sentences still misled her.

passage:
Vidya, don't look at me like that. I didn't lie to Mummy. I said I was at your place on Friday, and I was, for the first hour. Then your cousin's farewell party happened, and I just didn't mention it. Every sentence was true!
Anyway, yesterday Mummy saw a photo of us on your sister's status, balloons everywhere, music obviously loud. She didn't yell. She just said, "Jasleen, you gave me true sentences and a false picture." Then she went to make tea and didn't speak for ages.
Honestly, that was worse than yelling. I keep replaying it in my head on the way to school. I think she's right, and I hate that she's right. Would you have told your mum?

qa.q: Where did Mummy see the photo?
qa.a: Mummy saw the photo on Vidya's sister's status.

qa.q: What does Jasleen replaying Mummy's words suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Jasleen feels guilty and is starting to accept that leaving out the party misled Mummy, even though each sentence was true.

qa.q: What could Jasleen do now to repair things with Mummy?
qa.a: Jasleen could go to Mummy, admit the party was the part left out, and agree to share the whole plan before going out next time.

qa.q: How does Mummy see Jasleen's true sentences?
qa.a: Mummy sees that true sentences can still build a false picture, and she feels misled, which is why she goes quiet over her tea.

grounding: A teenager insists on being technically honest about being at Vidya's place, until Mummy points out the false picture the missing party created.

passage:
Anirban, sit, I have to tell someone. Last night, right, I was at Kritika's till nine, studying. Totally true. Then her cousin said there's a birthday party on the terrace of the next building, and we went up. Music, fairy lights, some college guys, everything.
This morning at breakfast, Mom goes, "How was Kritika's?" and I said, "Good, we finished the chemistry chapter." Also true! I didn't say one fake thing. I was like, Yamini, you're a genius.
But then she said, "I'm glad you have such a sensible friend," and gave me extra parathas. And I felt… sick. Like, properly sick.
Because if she knew about the terrace, she'd have wanted to know who was there, how I got home. She had a right to ask. I just made sure she couldn't.
So is it lying if every sentence is true? It feels like lying. What would you do?

qa.q: What did Yamini say at breakfast when asked about Kritika's?
qa.a: Yamini said, "Good, we finished the chemistry chapter."

qa.q: Why did Yamini feel sick after her mother gave her extra parathas?
qa.a: Yamini felt guilty, because Mom's trust and kindness were based on a picture that left out the terrace party.

qa.q: What would you advise Yamini to do now?
qa.a: Yamini could tell Mom about the party calmly, and next time share the whole plan so Mom can ask the questions she has a right to ask.

qa.q: What would change if Yamini's mother learned about the party from someone else?
qa.a: Mom would likely feel misled and trust Yamini less, even though no sentence was false.

grounding: It shows a teenager telling a parent true facts about a friend's house but leaving out the party, feeling technically honest while the parent is misled.

passage:
Saturday. Lokesh texted Papa: "At Amandeep's, studying." It was true at four. By eight, they were at a farmhouse birthday party on the highway with thirty people Lokesh barely knew. He got home at eleven and said, "We lost track of time."
Sunday. At breakfast Papa asked, "How's Amandeep doing with maths?" Lokesh talked for five minutes about trigonometry. Every sentence was real. Papa nodded, pleased.
The next Friday, Papa met Amandeep's father at the vegetable market. That evening he sat on Lokesh's bed. "Amandeep's father mentioned the farmhouse. On the highway. At night."
"I was at Amandeep's," Lokesh said. "I didn't lie."
"No," Papa said. "You chose what I got to know. If I'd known about the highway, I'd have wanted to pick you up. You took that away from me."
Lokesh looked at the floor. He had no answer.

qa.q: Where did Papa meet Amandeep's father?
qa.a: He met him at the vegetable market.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when Papa sat on his bed?
qa.a: He felt defensive at first and then ashamed, because Papa showed him that leaving out the party had misled him about his safety.

qa.q: What could Lokesh do differently the next time plans change?
qa.a: He could send Papa a quick message when the plan changes, saying where he is and asking for a pick-up if needed.

qa.q: How does Papa see the gap between Lokesh's words and what happened?
qa.a: Papa sees it as being misled, because the true words kept him from making a safety choice about the highway.

grounding: It shows a teenager giving a parent only true details about a friend's house while hiding the party, and the parent explaining how that misleads.

passage:
Indu, you think your Jagdish Chacha was always this boring, sensible man? Sit. At sixteen I told my mother, "I'm going to Bablu's house to study." And I did go. For one hour. Then Bablu and I took the last bus to the mela at the edge of town and stayed till midnight watching the giant wheel.
Next morning she asked, "How was studying?" I said, "Very good. Bablu's mother made halwa." True, true, all true. I was so proud of myself.
Then, on the way home, the bus driver told his wife, who told my aunt, who told my mother. My mother didn't scold. She only said, "If you had told me, I'd have given you money for the ride and made you promise to be back by ten. You didn't give me the chance."
That line stayed with me longer than any scolding.

qa.q: Where did young Jagdish and Bablu go after studying?
qa.a: They took the last bus to the mela at the edge of town.

qa.q: How did young Jagdish feel the morning after the mela?
qa.a: He felt proud and clever, believing that saying only true things meant he was honest.

qa.q: At which turning point in the story did Jagdish see the problem?
qa.a: When his mother said he had not given her the chance to set a time or pay for the ride, he saw that leaving out the mela had misled her.

qa.q: How might Jagdish's mother have felt when she heard about the mela from others?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and worried, because her son had been out till midnight without her knowing.

grounding: An uncle recalls telling his mother he was at a friend's house while leaving out the late mela, feeling honest while she was misled.

passage:
It was past ten and raining hard, and Devika's phone had died at eight. When she came in dripping, Papa was standing by the door with his own phone in his hand.
"Where were you? I called eleven times."
"At Aisha's. We did the chemistry project. Her mother made pasta." Every word was true.
She didn't say that at six they had all gone to Nikhil's birthday party two lanes away, with loud music and older boys she didn't know.
Her father, Farhan, sighed. "Okay. Charge your phone next time."
In her room Devika told herself she hadn't lied. But she felt hot all over. Papa had been scared for two hours, and he still didn't know where she had actually been when he was calling.
She sat on the bed for a long time. Then she went back out to the kitchen. "Papa, there's more. After Aisha's, we went to a party."

qa.q: How many times had Papa called?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: Why did Devika feel hot all over in her room?
qa.a: Devika felt guilty and uneasy, knowing every word was true but that Papa had still been misled about where she was.

qa.q: What did Devika do that turned it around?
qa.a: She went back to the kitchen and told Papa about the party after Aisha's, adding the missing part herself.

qa.q: What had those two hours been like for Farhan?
qa.a: Farhan was scared, calling eleven times with no answer, and still didn't know where his daughter had really been.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose every sentence was true while leaving out the party, feeling technically honest yet knowing her father was misled.
